items.output: 1→--- name: pdf description: Read, create, and transform PDF files. Covers pulling text and tables out of PDFs, generating new PDFs, merging and splitting documents, rotating pages, watermarking, encrypting or removing passwords, extracting embedded images, running OCR on scanned documents, and filling out PDF forms including official tax forms. Apply this skill whenever a task involves a .pdf file as input or deliverable. user-invocable: false --- # Working with PDFs Task-oriented recipes for PDF work, built around three Python libraries (`pypdf`, `pdfplumber`, `reportlab`) and the poppler-utils / qpdf command-line suites. 10→ Companion documents in this directory — open them when the task calls for it: - `forms.md` — required reading before filling out any PDF form - `tax.md` — required reading before preparing the official tax forms bundled under `forms/` - `reference.md` — deeper material: pypdfium2 rendering, JavaScript libraries (pdf-lib, pdfjs-dist), advanced qpdf/poppler flags, performance tuning, and troubleshooting ## Choosing a Tool | Goal | Reach for | 20→|------|-----------| | Pull out plain text | `pdfplumber` or `pdftotext` | | Pull out tables | `pdfplumber` (`extract_tables`) | | Combine documents | `pypdf` or `qpdf` | | Break a document apart | `pypdf` (one writer per output) | | Produce a new PDF | `reportlab` (Canvas for absolute layout, Platypus for flowing documents) | | Grab embedded images | `pdfimages` | | Render pages as pictures | `pdftoppm` / `pdf2image` | | OCR a scanned document | `pytesseract` + `pdf2image` | | Fill out a form | see `forms.md` | 30→ ## Getting Content Out of a PDF ### Text ```python import pdfplumber with pdfplumber.open("report.pdf") as doc: full_text = "\n".join(pg.extract_text() or "" for pg in doc.pages) 40→``` From the shell, `pdftotext` is quickest; `-layout` keeps the visual column structure and `-f`/`-l` bound the page range: ```bash pdftotext -layout report.pdf report.txt pdftotext -f 2 -l 4 report.pdf middle_pages.txt ``` ### Tables 50→ `pdfplumber` returns each table as a list of rows; feed them straight into pandas when you need to reshape or export: ```python import pandas as pd import pdfplumber frames = [] with pdfplumber.open("report.pdf") as doc: for pg in doc.pages: 60→ for tbl in pg.extract_tables(): if tbl: frames.append(pd.DataFrame(tbl[1:], columns=tbl[0])) if frames: pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True).to_excel("tables.xlsx", index=False) ``` ### Document Metadata 70→```python from pypdf import PdfReader info = PdfReader("report.pdf").metadata for key in ("title", "author", "subject", "creator"): print(key, "=", getattr(info, key)) ``` ### Embedded Images vs. Page Renders 80→These are different operations — pick the right one: - `pdfimages -all report.pdf img/fig` copies the *original bitmap objects* embedded in the file, untouched by page layout. - `pdftoppm -png -r 300 report.pdf pages/pg` *rasterizes* whole pages — text, vectors, and annotations included — producing what is effectively a screenshot of each page. A rendered page is never a substitute for an extracted image, and vice versa. ### Scanned Documents (OCR) Scanned PDFs contain pictures of text, so extraction tools return nothing useful. Rasterize first, then OCR each page: 90→ ```python # pip install pytesseract pdf2image import pytesseract from pdf2image import convert_from_path pages = convert_from_path("scan.pdf") recognized = [pytesseract.image_to_string(img) for img in pages] print("\n\n".join(recognized)) ``` 100→ ## Reorganizing Pages ### Combine Documents ```python from pypdf import PdfWriter writer = PdfWriter() for path in ["intro.pdf", "body.pdf", "appendix.pdf"]: 110→ writer.append(path) with open("combined.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` Or from the shell: ```bash qpdf --empty --pages intro.pdf body.pdf appendix.pdf -- combined.pdf 120→``` ### Split into Pieces ```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter src = PdfReader("combined.pdf") for idx, pg in enumerate(src.pages, start=1): part = PdfWriter() 130→ part.add_page(pg) with open(f"part_{idx}.pdf", "wb") as out: part.write(out) ``` `qpdf` handles page ranges without any code: ```bash qpdf combined.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- first_five.pdf ``` 140→ ### Rotate ```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter src = PdfReader("sideways.pdf") writer = PdfWriter() for pg in src.pages: writer.add_page(pg) 150→writer.pages[0].rotate(90) # clockwise degrees; must be a multiple of 90 with open("upright.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` ### Stamp a Watermark Overlay one PDF page (the watermark) onto every page of another: 160→```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter stamp = PdfReader("stamp.pdf").pages[0] src = PdfReader("contract.pdf") writer = PdfWriter() for pg in src.pages: pg.merge_page(stamp) writer.add_page(pg) 170→ with open("stamped.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` ### Passwords ```python from pypdf import PdfWriter 180→writer = PdfWriter() writer.append("private.pdf") writer.encrypt(user_password="open-me", owner_password="admin-key") with open("locked.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` Removing a known password is a one-liner: 190→```bash qpdf --password=open-me --decrypt locked.pdf unlocked.pdf ``` ## Generating PDFs with reportlab Two APIs, two mindsets: - **Canvas** — you place every element at explicit coordinates. The origin is the *bottom-left* corner of the page and y grows upward, so "1 inch from the top" is `page_height - inch - element_height`. - **Platypus** — you build a `story` list of flowables (`Paragraph`, `Table`, `Image`, `Spacer`, `PageBreak`) and the layout engine paginates for you. Prefer this for anything document-like. 200→ ### Minimal Examples ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas c = canvas.Canvas("note.pdf", pagesize=letter) _, page_h = letter c.drawString(72, page_h - 72, "Placed one inch from the top-left corner.") 210→c.line(72, page_h - 90, 400, page_h - 90) c.save() ``` ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet from reportlab.platypus import PageBreak, Paragraph, SimpleDocTemplate, Spacer styles = getSampleStyleSheet() 220→story = [ Paragraph("Annual Summary", styles["Title"]), Spacer(1, 12), Paragraph("Body text flows and wraps automatically. " * 15, styles["Normal"]), PageBreak(), Paragraph("Second Section", styles["Heading1"]), ] SimpleDocTemplate("summary.pdf", pagesize=letter).build(story) ``` 230→### Placing Images Keep the aspect ratio: derive the missing dimension from the source image, or let reportlab do it when fitting a box. ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.units import inch from reportlab.lib.utils import ImageReader from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas 240→c = canvas.Canvas("figure.pdf", pagesize=letter) _, page_h = letter src = ImageReader("chart.png") src_w, src_h = src.getSize() w = 4.5 * inch h = w * src_h / src_w # bottom-left origin: subtract the image height to hang it below the top margin c.drawImage(src, inch, page_h - inch - h, width=w, height=h) 250→c.save() ``` To fit an image inside a fixed region without distortion: ```python c.drawImage("photo.jpg", box_x, box_y, width=box_w, height=box_h, preserveAspectRatio=True, anchor="c") ``` 260→In Platypus, images are flowables — size them yourself and let the engine position them: ```python from reportlab.platypus import Image pic = Image("logo.png", width=w, height=h, hAlign="CENTER") story.append(pic) ``` Prefer `drawImage` over `drawInlineImage`; it registers the image once as a shared object, so repeated use is smaller and faster. 270→ ### Subscripts and Superscripts Do **not** type Unicode sub/superscript characters (₂, ⁹, …) — reportlab's built-in fonts lack those glyphs and they render as black rectangles. Use inline markup inside a `Paragraph` instead: ```python Paragraph("H2O and E = mc2", styles["Normal"]) ``` When drawing directly on a Canvas (no `Paragraph`), simulate the effect by shrinking the font and shifting the baseline manually. 280→ ### Tables Two non-negotiable rules, both consequences of how `Table` lays out cells: 1. **Every cell — headers included — goes inside a `Paragraph`.** Bare strings never wrap; long values run over neighboring cells or off the page. `Paragraph` cells also accept inline markup (``, ``, ``, ``). 2. **Pass explicit `colWidths`, sized by content.** Equal-width columns squeeze prose and waste space on short IDs. Budget most of the printable width (letter with 1" margins ≈ 6.5", landscape ≈ 9") to the prose-heavy columns. ```python from reportlab.lib import colors 290→from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet from reportlab.lib.units import inch from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph, SimpleDocTemplate, Table, TableStyle body = getSampleStyleSheet()["BodyText"] rows = [ [Paragraph("ID", body), Paragraph("Name", body), Paragraph("Notes", body)], [Paragraph("1", body), Paragraph("Widget", body), 300→ Paragraph("Long prose wraps cleanly inside its column instead of spilling over.", body)], ] grid = Table(rows, colWidths=[0.5 * inch, 1.5 * inch, 4.5 * inch], repeatRows=1) grid.setStyle(TableStyle([ ("GRID", (0, 0), (-1, -1), 0.5, colors.grey), ("VALIGN", (0, 0), (-1, -1), "TOP"), ("BACKGROUND", (0, 0), (-1, 0), colors.lightgrey), ])) 310→SimpleDocTemplate("grid.pdf", pagesize=letter).build([grid]) ``` Also: `repeatRows=1` reprints the header when a table crosses a page break; `VALIGN TOP` keeps wrapped rows tidy; and when content is genuinely too wide, switch to `landscape(letter)` rather than shrinking columns into illegibility. ## Always Verify Visually After producing or modifying any PDF — especially after filling form fields, where name-to-label mappings are frequently wrong — render each page and look at it: ```bash 320→pdftoppm -png -r 300 -f 1 -l 1 result.pdf /tmp/check pdftoppm -png -r 300 -f 2 -l 2 result.pdf /tmp/check_p2 ``` pdftoppm appends the page number to the output prefix, so these commands write `/tmp/check-1.png` and `/tmp/check_p2-2.png`. View each PNG and confirm every value sits beside its intended label, nothing overlaps, and nothing is clipped. Inspecting the raw PDF objects cannot catch these problems; rendering does. ## Forms and Tax Forms - Any form-filling task: read `forms.md` first and follow its steps in order. It covers both PDFs with real fillable fields and flat/scanned forms that need positioned text annotations, with helper scripts under `scripts/`. - Tax returns: read `tax.md`. The deliverable is always the official IRS form from `forms/`, filled in — never a homemade summary document. 330→

1→INFO123 Project: Build a Business with AI

Overview
Generative AI tools, such as Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT and Mistral are becoming essential
business tools which, if used wisely, can augment human cognitive abilities and productivity.
For this project, you will use generative AI to build a breakfast products business from
scratch.

You will use generative AI to do the following:
10→
   -   Create a breakfast product
   -   Analyse and visualize market data
   -   Create a company
   -   Develop a marketing strategy, including product packaging and launch advertisement
   -   Define KPIs for the core business processes
   -   Model strategic information systems and core data
   -   Develop a customer support chatbot
   -   Develop the business' web page using a vibe-coding agent

20→You will use this information to create a finalized business plan and a video presentation (2
to 3 minutes max). In this presentation, you will pitch your new business to investors and
you will discuss your experience in using AI for creating your business.


Deliverables to be submitted to LEARN
   ●   A comprehensive, polished business plan document (a collection of artefacts from
       the business creation tasks, packaged into a single PDF document) - see task 13
   ●   A short advertisement jingle (15-30 sec., via an audio file .mp3) - see task 8
   ●   A customer support chatbot (a working URL) - see task 11
30→   ●   A demo of a website (a working URL) - see task 12
   ●   A video presentation of business pitch and lessons learned about working with AI for
       this assignment (via a video file .mp4 or .mov only – no links) - see task 14
   ●   A log of all chat session URLs (via the submission form on Learn)


Due Date & Submission
16 October 2026 5pm


40→

2026-S2                                                                                         1
 Instructions
The pages that follow contain a step-by-step guide for creating the content of the business
plan for your breakfast products business. You are expected to be creative, go beyond
these instructions and examples by applying the techniques covered in the lectures and in
the labs, and push the boundaries of AI capabilities.


50→Essential Workflow Practices
1. Use multiple chat sessions: To avoid “context rot” (when the AI loses track of earlier
context in long conversations), create one chat session per task or group of related tasks.
For example:

   -   One chat for market data analysis (Task 2)
   -   One chat for product development (Tasks 3-4)
   -   One chat for marketing strategy (Tasks 7-8)
   -   And so on...

60→2. Keep track of your work in a project folder on your computer: Set up a dedicated
folder on your computer to log and store all content produced by the AI as you progress
through the tasks. In this folder, organise:

   -   Content generated by AI (paste it in text files or Word documents)
   -   Data analyses and figures
   -   Images (logos, product packaging, social media ads)
   -   Audio files (jingles)
   -   Image files of process diagrams and data models
   -   Personal notes and reflections: keep track of key decisions you made about your
70→       business

You will need these materials to create your final business plan and video presentation.

3. Keep a log of ALL links to your chats: Use your AI tool's share function to generate
permanent URLs for each chat session. You need to submit all chat links via a form on
Learn, and flag 2–3 sessions that show your best work with AI. When choosing which
sessions to flag, pick ones that show how you steered the AI and how you checked its
claims against a real source. DOUBLE-CHECK THAT THE URLs ARE ACCESSIBLE.

80→4. Save and export everything: Don't rely solely on chat history. Copy or download all
outputs locally:

   -   Export images and diagrams as files
   -   Copy and paste text into documents
   -   Save audio files

Chat sessions can be deleted or lost, so maintain your own copies.


90→                                                                                              2
 Your Tasks

Task 1: Create First Product Ideas
Begin by working with the AI to generate ideas for your first breakfast product, tailored to
your preferences. The breakfast products category typically includes 4 sub-categories:
breakfast cereals, nutritional cereal bars, spreads, and liquid breakfasts.

Prompt the AI to ask you interactive questions about the kind of breakfast product you want
to create to generate product ideas.
100→



Task 2: Analyse current market trends
You obtained some data on past breakfast product trends in New Zealand. Use the AI to
identify potential opportunities for launching a new breakfast product.

Download the Excel dataset nz_breakfast_sales_2022_2025.xlsx from Learn.

110→   1. Upload the dataset to a chat and ask the AI to identify, report, and explain data
      quality issues.

   2. Work with the AI to fix any data quality issues it has found.

   3. Ask the AI to analyse and visualise key aspects of the data to inform your market
      research.

Store the results of each step in your project log and folder, including any figures you have
produced with the AI.
120→



Task 3: Finalise your product
Finalise your first product and determine the flavour and recipe.

   1. Prompt the AI to combine your breakfast product preferences and the results of the
      data analysis to determine what you should create for your first breakfast product

130→   2. Brainstorm and identify a name for your first breakfast product.

   3. Determine the possible flavour(s) of the breakfast product.




                                                                                                3
    4. Next, create a recipe to produce the breakfast product.

140→   5. The recipe will likely be designed to be made at home; ask the AI to provide an
      industrial version of this recipe that can be produced at scale and at low cost. You
      can ask the AI for additional constraints or business requirements that fit your
      business strategy.

   6. Generate a brief product description.

           ●   Example prompt: Based on the discussion so far, create a brief product
               description.

150→Record the results of each step in your project folder.




Task 4: Critique and refine your product idea
It's time to get some feedback on your product idea.

   1. Create a document that summarises the breakfast product information you produced
      in Task 3. With your prompt, upload the traces you have collected in Task 3.
160→
           ●   Example prompt: Create a document that summarizes my breakfast product,

   2. Upload the summary document into a new chat and ask the AI to assess the various

           ●   Example prompt: Attached is a new breakfast product idea. Analyse the

170→               and uniqueness, consumer appeal, brand and marketing potential, and

Record the results of each step in your project folder.




Task 5: Gather intelligence on market competitors
180→Research the competitive landscape to understand how your product compares to existing
offerings in the market.

   1. Search online for the nearest competitors.




                                                                                               4
            ●   Example prompt: Search online for the competitive landscape, and what are
190→               the nearest products to mine? How much do they charge? What is my

   2. After you finish the search, be sure to unselect the web search feature to avoid

   3. Ask the AI to analyse your product's differentiation compared to competitors.

   4. Identify 2-3 key competitors and record their:

200→           -   Product names and descriptions
           -   Pricing
           -   Target customers
           -   Key selling points
           -   Your competitive advantages

Record the results of each step in your project folder.



210→
Task 6: Create a company name and logo
   1. It's time to pick a company name. To receive suggestions from the AI, provide some
      information about your product and what your company should be about. Ask the AI

   2. Now generate a logo for your company.

           ●   Tip 1: In the AI, click on the "Tools" button and then "Create Image". You can
220→               also use one of the free tools we list on p., but your ability to iterate and refine
               the logo might be more limited because of lower usage limits.

           ●   Tip 2: Use fast models for prototyping images and thinking models for final
               output: A kind reminder to pay attention to your usage limit; generating
               images may result in faster model usage. If you generate too many images,
               you may exceed the usage limit and be unable to generate any more. Use
               cheap and faster generation with smaller (non-thinking) models to develop
               and iterate your image prompt. Once you have locked in your image design,
               then use the thinking or pro mode to generate a higher quality output. The
230→               thinking mode will use up your credits faster.

           ●   Note: Image generation often contains spelling mistakes, as the model
               generates pixels rather than words written on an image. Models are improving
               quickly, but this remains a limitation of existing image generation technology.

Save the results of each step in your project log and folder.


                                                                                                  5
240→ Task 7: Target customer and packaging
After developing the initial product, identify a target customer segment and develop a
packaging prototype.

   1. Begin by identifying a customer segment that is most likely to purchase the breakfast
      product. A customer segment is a specific group of potential buyers who share
      similar characteristics, needs, or behaviours; they are the most likely to purchase the
      breakfast product.

   2. Based on this information about the customer segment, generate an image of a
250→      product package design. This should be an image that realistically depicts the

   3. Get feedback: ask the AI to provide synthetic customer feedback on your ideas. In a

           ●   Tip: A common strategy for improving the outputs is to specify a persona for
260→               the AI. Instead of just asking the AI “You are a customer...” describe a person
               with specific goals and hurdles, such as “You are a time-crunched parent
               looking for low-sugar options” or “You are a fitness enthusiast focused on

   4. Incorporate the feedback into your product package design and regenerate an image

Save the results of each step in your project folder.

270→


Task 8: Online marketing strategy
With the information you have gathered so far, create a marketing strategy that includes
ideas for social media and podcast advertisement.

   1. Provide the AI with the content and images you created in Task 4, 5 and 7. Ask the

280→
   2. Ask the AI to criticize its work. Based on its suggestions, improve the draft product

            ●   Tip: You can provide more information about the type of tone and other

290→               prompt: Use a more formal tone or use a more playful tone.

   3. Design a potential social media advertisement for this product.

           ●   Start by ask the AI to identify the appropriate channels: What social media

   5. Create a 15- to 30-second jingle/song to advertise your product on podcasts.

           ●   Example prompt: Create a 15-second jingle to go with the advertising

310→           ●   Tip: In your prompt, specify the vibe and genre of the music: energetic,

320→
   6. Ask the AI to identify New Zealand podcasts that would be good channels to

Save the outputs of each step in your project folder.

 FAQ

Q: Can I edit the AI outputs or should I let the AI do everything?

880→A: The goal of the project is to develop your skills in using AI effectively. Therefore, the
question you should ask yourself is: what approach will likely yield the best outcome?
Letting the AI do all the work by itself is unlikely to be the most optimal approach to get a
good result out of it. If you think you need to intervene or customise the content while you
work with an AI, that's absolutely fine - and it's likely to make the outcome better. That's true
for any task you may do with AI, not just the task of creating and putting together a report.

Q: Sometimes when I want to get a sharing link for my Gemini chat transcript the link
is greyed out. What should I do?

prompts and Gemini’s answers. Submit the Word file along with your video on Learn, and
indicate in the chat form that you submitted a file that contains the transcript of your chat.

Q: I created my chatbot as a gem in Gemini. I can't get it to work in incognito mode.

A: You must be logged in to a Google account for a gem to work. To test it, you should log in
or share it with another user who is logged in. You do not have to rebuild your chat bot in
another model.

900→Q: I created my chatbot in ChatGPT. I can't get it to work in incognito mode.

A: You must be logged in to ChatGPT for the GPT agent to work. To test it, you should log in
or share it with another user who is logged in. You do not have to rebuild your chatbot in
another model.

Q: I asked the AI to produce a PDF but it won't do it.

A: If the AI won't produce a pdf directly, ask it explicitly to make a Google Docs or Word
document. Then you can edit and save the document yourself as a PDF.
910→
Q: How should I get the AI to insert the images and Mermaid diagram into my plan?

A: You should ask the AI to make a placeholder where the images and diagram need to go
in the document. Then you can paste them into that place yourself.

Q: Do I need to submit the project folder mentioned in “Essential Workflow
Practices”?

A: No, the brief only suggests creating a folder on your computer to organise your workflow
920→and keep track of the outputs you create with the AI.

import zipfile
from xml.etree import ElementTree as ET
z = zipfile.ZipFile('nz_breakfast_sales_2022_2025.xlsx')
ns = {'m':'http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/spreadsheetml/2006/main',
      'r':'http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships'}
wb = ET.fromstring(z.read('xl/workbook.xml'))
sheets = [(s.attrib['name'], s.attrib['{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships}id']) for s in wb.findall('m:sheets/m:sheet', ns)]
print('SHEETS', sheets)
rels = ET.fromstring(z.read('xl/_rels/workbook.xml.rels'))
rid_to_target = {}
for rel in rels:
    rid_to_target[rel.attrib['Id']] = rel.attrib['Target']
# shared strings
ss = []
if 'xl/sharedStrings.xml' in z.namelist():
    root = ET.fromstring(z.read('xl/sharedStrings.xml'))
    for si in root.findall('m:si', ns):
        texts = [t.text or '' for t in si.iter('{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/spreadsheetml/2006/main}t')]
        ss.append(''.join(texts))
print('shared strings', len(ss))
for name, rid in sheets:
    target = rid_to_target[rid]
    if not target.startswith('xl/'):
        target = 'xl/' + target
    root = ET.fromstring(z.read(target))
    rows = root.findall('m:sheetData/m:row', ns)
    print('---', name, 'rows', len(rows))
    def cell_val(c):
        t = c.attrib.get('t')
        v = c.find('m:v', ns)
        if v is None or v.text is None:
            is_el = c.find('m:is', ns)
            if is_el is not None:
                return ''.join(t.text or '' for t in is_el.iter('{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/spreadsheetml/2006/main}t'))
            return ''
        if t == 's':
            return ss[int(v.text)]
        return v.text
    for row in rows[:12]:
        vals = []
        for c in row.findall('m:c', ns):
            vals.append(f"{c.attrib.get('r','')}:{cell_val(c)}")
        print(' | '.join(vals)[:400])

for si in root.findall('m:si', ns):
    texts = [t.text or '' for t in si.iter('{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/spreadsheetml/2006/main}t')]

sheet = ET.fromstring(z.read('xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml'))

def cell_val(c):
    t = c.attrib.get('t')
    v = c.find('m:v', ns)
    if v is None or v.text is None:
        return None
    if t == 's':
        return ss[int(v.text)]
    return v.text

headers = None
data = []
for i, row in enumerate(rows):
    vals = {}
    for c in row.findall('m:c', ns):
        ref = c.attrib.get('r','')
        col = ''.join(ch for ch in ref if ch.isalpha())
        vals[col] = cell_val(c)
    if i == 0:
        headers = vals
        continue
    data.append(vals)

cols = ['A','B','C','D','E','F','G','H','I','J','K','L','M','N','O']
print('N', len(data))
print('HEADERS', [headers[c] for c in cols])
# missing
for c in cols:
    miss = sum(1 for r in data if r.get(c) in (None, ''))
    if miss:
        print('MISSING', headers[c], miss)

def uniq(col):
    return Counter(r.get(col) for r in data)

print('DATES', sorted(uniq('A')))
print('CATEGORIES', uniq('D'))
print('SEGMENTS', uniq('L'))
print('TIERS', uniq('M'))
print('BRANDS', len(uniq('C')), 'PRODUCTS', len(uniq('B')))
print('FLAGS plant', uniq('E'))
print('weight conscious', uniq('F'))
print('performance', uniq('G'))
print('gluten', uniq('H'))
print('organic', uniq('I'))

# numeric issues
bad_price = bad_units = bad_rev = zero_both = zero_units_pos_rev = pos_units_zero_rev = 0
mismatch = 0
neg = 0
price_vals = []
weights = Counter()
for r in data:
    try:
        price = float(r['J']); units = float(r['N']); rev = float(r['O'])
    except Exception:
        bad_price += 1
        continue
    price_vals.append(price)
    weights[r.get('K')] += 1
    if price < 0 or units < 0 or rev < 0:
        neg += 1
    if units == 0 and rev == 0:
        zero_both += 1
    if units == 0 and rev != 0:
        zero_units_pos_rev += 1
    if units != 0 and rev == 0:
        pos_units_zero_rev += 1
    # expected revenue thousands = price * units_thousands
    if units != 0:
        expected = price * units
        if abs(expected - rev) / max(abs(expected), 0.01) > 0.05:

print('negatives', neg)
print('zero units and rev', zero_both)
print('zero units nonzero rev', zero_units_pos_rev)
print('nonzero units zero rev', pos_units_zero_rev)
print('price*units vs revenue >5% off', mismatch)
print('price min/max', min(price_vals), max(price_vals))
print('unique weights', len(weights))
print('sample odd weights', [w for w in weights if w and ('g' not in str(w).lower() and 'ml' not in str(w).lower())][:20])

# duplicate product+date
seen = Counter((r['A'], r['B'], r['C']) for r in data)
dups = sum(1 for k,v in seen.items() if v>1)
print('duplicate product-brand-quarter keys', dups)

# product appearing in multiple categories or brands
prod_cat = defaultdict(set)
prod_brand = defaultdict(set)
prod_price = defaultdict(set)
for r in data:
    prod_cat[r['B']].add(r['D'])
    prod_brand[r['B']].add(r['C'])
    prod_price[r['B']].add(r['J'])
multi_cat = sum(1 for s in prod_cat.values() if len(s)>1)
multi_brand = sum(1 for s in prod_brand.values() if len(s)>1)
multi_price = sum(1 for s in prod_price.values() if len(s)>1)
print('products multi category', multi_cat, 'multi brand name collision', multi_brand, 'multi price', multi_price)

# blank names
blank_name = sum(1 for r in data if not r.get('B'))
print('blank product', blank_name)

# revenue total
rev_sum = sum(float(r['O']) for r in data if r.get('O') not in (None,''))
units_sum = sum(float(r['N']) for r in data if r.get('N') not in (None,''))
print('total units thousands', round(units_sum,1), 'total revenue thousands NZD', round(rev_sum,1))

# category x year revenue
by = defaultdict(float)
for r in data:
    year = str(r['A'])[:4]
    by[(year, r['D'])] += float(r['O'] or 0)
print('REVENUE BY YEAR/CAT (thousands NZD)')
for k in sorted(by):
    print(k, round(by[k],1))

Duplicate records share identical product names, brands, and quarters but differ in pack sizes.

The natural key is Date, Product Name, Brand, and Weight. Price tier conflicts also exist within these groups. I will document this in the data spec to prevent task 2 from wrongly deleting distinct pack sizes. Now drafting the full project plan in a markdown file.

The plan will target an A+ grade. It will define deliverables, dataset schema, data quality issues, and required artefacts. Website, chatbot, video, and jingle specs are included. Folder structure and session log standards are also defined. The recommended stack and working rules are mapped out. Tasks 1 through 14 are sequenced into phases with inputs, outputs, and completion criteria.

The product will not be locked in until the user answers preference questions. A decision gate is added at the start of the plan. The deadline is 16 October 2026, giving roughly sixteen days. The schedule will be mapped to this calendar window.

The sixteen-day schedule is now mapped to specific tasks. Days one through two cover setup and initial data. Days three through four focus on product selection, critique, and competitor research. Days five through six handle brand identity, packaging, marketing, and the jingle. Days seven through eight build operations and the entity-relationship diagram. Days nine through ten are reserved for the chatbot and website. Days eleven through thirteen produce the business plan PDF. Days fourteen through fifteen cover slides and video. Day sixteen is a submission buffer.

Excellence criteria are built into the workflow. Prompting and steering will use flagged sessions with pushback, personas, constraints, adversarial review, and context carry-forward. Verification requires checking factual claims against independent sources such as competitor prices, New Zealand manufacturers, podcasts, and nutrition claims.

Integration criteria require one consistent voice and unified visuals across all artefacts. Reflection Q1 is personal; Q2 must be written by the student, not the AI.

The plan must be transparent about tooling. The course assesses shareable chat URLs from Gemini, Mistral, or ChatGPT. This session runs on Grok. The plan will serve as the operating document for the student's own AI sessions.

The workspace will serve as a local project folder for canonical artefacts. Grok can generate data cleaning scripts, Mermaid diagrams, PDFs, and website code here. The graded chat evidence must still live in Gemini, Mistral, or ChatGPT with public share links.

The website must be publicly accessible without login. Figma Make is recommended for its design-to-code workflow.

A local static site hosted on GitHub Pages or Cloudflare is a viable alternative to Figma Make. It satisfies the public, login-free URL requirement and gives the student full control over deployment. The plan will list this as a concrete technical option alongside the recommended design-to-code workflow.

The chatbot will be a hosted Gem or Custom GPT. Its system prompt will be drawn from the project knowledge files. Building a custom AI is avoided to keep the URL story simple and openable by markers.

The business plan will be 1500 to 2500 words and written in an investor-ready style.

The business plan will follow a structured eleven-section format. It opens with a cover page and executive summary. The product section covers name, flavour, description, recipe differences between home and industrial scales, and differentiation. Market analysis will present New Zealand breakfast figures from 2022 to 2025 and opportunity. Competitor intelligence will profile two or three rivals. The target customer segment follows. Marketing strategy will detail channels, ad image, jingle, and NZ podcast usage. Operations will specify the New Zealand manufacturer, core processes, a critical process diagram, and bottlenecks. Information systems will map entities, KPIs, the ERD, and how data supports decisions. Commercial viability scores from task four will close the document.

The business plan will close with a brief investor ask and next steps. Required images are embedded in the context: market research figures, logo, packaging, social ad, process diagram, and ERD. Word count excludes images.

The folder structure is now defined. It includes PLAN.md, a session log, a data folder with the raw spreadsheet, cleaned CSV, and quality notes, a research folder for task files, a brand folder for visual assets, a marketing folder for strategy, jingle, and podcast files, and an operations folder.

The folder structure is now fully detailed. Operations will contain manufacturer notes, a Mermaid process diagram, its PNG export, and bottlenecks. Information systems will hold entity and KPI definitions, the ERD in Mermaid, and its PNG. The chatbot folder will store the system prompt, test log, and public URL. Presentation materials will include slides, notes, and the student-written reflection notes. A central chat-log file will record all AI interactions.

Diagrams must be rendered as Mermaid flowcharts for processes and Mermaid erDiagrams for the entity relationship model. PNG exports need sufficient resolution for PDF embedding, with render errors fixed before saving. A schema table will define the data technical specification.

Task 2 requires the student to verify data quality in a logged chat. The scan must not be treated as the submitted analysis. Three issues stand out. Unit and revenue columns are often missing together. Over twenty-nine rows show implausible unit prices above forty dollars. Revenue and units remain coherent so those rows should not be dropped. Eight hundred sixty-eight product-brand-quarter groups appear in the data. Most are different pack weights or SKUs. Only about four are exact duplicates. Deduplication must not rely on product name alone.

Sixteen rows show price multiplied by units diverging from revenue by more than five percent. Most of these are the corrupted price rows.

The panel is balanced with roughly seven hundred fifty-one rows across sixteen quarters. Flags are clean binary values.

Categories include bars, cereals, spreads, and liquid breakfasts. There are ninety-five brands and six hundred sixty-two product names. Segments split into branded and private label tiers: value, standard, and premium.

Revenue and unit figures are in thousands of New Zealand dollars.

Four charts are recommended for the business plan. Two to three should be embedded. The first shows revenue by category over time. The second shows revenue or share by price tier, plant-powered status, or other attributes. The third compares growth rates between 2022 and 2025.

A fourth chart will highlight a white-space attribute combination that is growing but under-supplied.

Verification sources for excellence claims are now defined. Competitor prices should be checked on supermarket or brand websites. Manufacturer details should come from company websites. Podcast existence should be confirmed through podcast platforms or Apple and Spotify listings. Nutrition and recipe claims must align with MPI and Food Standards Australia New Zealand labelling rules when health claims are made. Any market size figure stated by the AI that is not computed directly from the spreadsheet requires independent verification.

The plan now specifies three excellence-flagging sessions. Task 2 will include a second spreadsheet verification. Task 4 or 5 will pair adversarial competitor critique with a retailer price check. Task 8 or 9 will cover marketing critique or manufacturer verification.

Each session will target one task group. A product one-pager brief will carry into the next session rather than one giant chat.

Before task 3 locks, the user must answer four personal questions: dietary constraints and preferences, category leanings, brand personality, and price position.

The video will run three minutes and twenty-nine seconds. The pitch is capped at one minute. Reflection covers the first two questions. The target finish time is two minutes and fifty seconds.

The pitch needs two slides. Reflection needs two to four slides. The student writes all reflection slides.

The business plan uses one authorial voice. Jacob reviews every section. A fact-check table will verify claims.

A definition-of-done checklist will map core and excellence requirements. The file will be named PLAN.md in the project root. Drafting will use polished markdown with direct affirmative language and no contrastive negation. A recommended local website build specification will also be included.

The website will be a static landing page with no login. It will display the company name, logo, product, short description, and how to buy or join a waitlist. Packaging colours must remain consistent. A product page and cart are optional for core deliverables.

If built in this repository, it will be a single HTML and CSS file deployed via GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, or Netlify. Testing should happen in a private window.

The chatbot will be a public Gem or Custom GPT. Its system prompt will contain multiple sections. Knowledge files will include the product one-pager, FAQ, ingredients, and where to buy. Fictional retail locations may be used for planned distribution, but no real stockist should be invented.

A test question list will be prepared for the chatbot. Login to Google or ChatGPT is acceptable per the FAQ, but the website must remain publicly accessible without authentication.

The jingle must be an MP3 between twenty and forty seconds long, under a minute maximum, and must relate to the product. Lyrics should also be saved as plain text. It can be generated with Gemini music or tools like Suno or ElevenLabs.

The business plan PDF should run between fifteen hundred and two thousand five hundred words excluding images. All six image types must be embedded. The document should use one consistent professional style and be exported from Word or Google Docs using a placeholder method before pasting final images.

A context-brief template will be added so the user can paste it at the start of each new chat to carry session context forward. A verification log template will also be included. The plan is now complete.

I will write PLAN.md directly into the project root rather than using the plan mode tool. This avoids potential file location issues and ensures the markdown deliverable is exactly where the user expects it.

The plan is due Friday 16 October 2026 at 5pm. The current date is 30 September 2026.

The project will be split into seven phases. Setup and preferences run 30 September to 1 October. Tasks one through two follow 1–3 October. Tasks three through five run 4–6 October. Tasks six through eight cover brand, packaging, marketing, and jingle from 7–9 October. Tasks nine through ten handle operations and ERD on 10–11 October. Tasks eleven through twelve build the chatbot and website on 12–13 October. The business plan PDF is due on 14 October.

Phase 7 runs 15 October for the final slides and recording. Phase 8 is 16 October morning, with URL tests and submission by 5pm. The plan will advise assembling sections continuously so the draft is ready for editing by 14 October rather than writing from scratch. The product decision remains a gate that must be answered by the user. Reflection notes must be written in a file and not pasted into an AI chat.

The reflection worksheet will contain only the questions from the brief, with no sample answers. The plan will remain strictly procedural and technical, avoiding any fabricated business content. Each task will include a definition of done that specifies inputs, outputs, file paths, and acceptance checks.

The final reply will present a concise, readable version of the plan alongside the full file. The file will contain templates and detailed sections that are too lengthy for a chat response.

The assignment is a full breakfast-business build with a fixed set of artefacts and a specification-grading scheme. I’ll write that into a project plan with the data schema, deliverable specs, and a dated task sequence.

# INFO123 Project Plan — Build a Breakfast Business with AI

**Course:** INFO123, 2026 Semester 2
**Assignment weight:** 25%
**Due:** Friday 16 October 2026, 5:00 pm, via Learn
**Workspace:** this folder is the project log. Learn does not require the folder itself. It is where every artefact is saved so nothing depends on chat history.

This plan is the operating document for the assignment described in `INFO123 Project - Build a Business with AI - Instructions.pdf` and graded by `INFO123 Project - Marking Guide.pdf`. It specifies what “done” means for every deliverable, then sequences the work from 30 September to submission.

The product itself is not chosen in this plan. Task 1 of the brief requires the product to come from your preferences plus the New Zealand sales data. Locking a product before that conversation would skip the assessed workflow.

---

## 1. What has to exist on 16 October

| # | Deliverable | Format | Pass condition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Video | `.mp4` or `.mov` file uploaded to Learn. A link is a fail. | Plays, talking-head, 2–3 minutes, hard stop 3:29. Pitch ≤ 1 minute, then personal reflection. |
| 2 | Chat session log | URLs in the Learn form | Every working session listed. 2–3 sessions flagged. Missing this log is an E. |
| 3 | Business plan | One PDF | All 13 task sections represented, about 1,500–2,500 words excluding images, six required image types embedded in context. |
| 4 | Jingle | `.mp3` | Plays, 15–60 seconds, clearly about the product. Aim for 20–40 seconds. |
| 5 | Website | Public URL in the Learn form | Loads with no login and shows at least a landing page for the product. |
| 6 | Chatbot | Public URL in the Learn form | Loads and answers at least one product question. A Gemini or ChatGPT login is acceptable. A login wall on the website is not. |

Missing the video is 0/25. Missing the chat-log form is an E (7.5/25). Missing one of items 3–6 is a C−. Missing two of items 3–6 is a D.

### How a higher grade is earned

Core completion lands in the C range (C = 14.25/25). Each excellence criterion below is met or not met. The band is the count of criteria met. Plus and minus inside a band depend on how strongly they are met.

| Excellence criteria met | Band | Mark out of 25 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | C | 14.25 (C+ 15.50, C− 13.00) |
| 1–2 | B | 18.00 (B+ 19.25, B− 16.75) |
| 3–4 | A | 21.75 (A− 20.50) |
| 5 | A+ | 23.75–25 |

| # | Criterion | Where it is judged | What “met” requires |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Prompting and steering | 2 of the flagged chats | You push back, demand revisions, and use techniques beyond the brief’s example prompts: a persona with goals and constraints, tone or format constraints, an adversarial review, meta-prompting, or context carried from an earlier session. |
| 2 | Verification and judgment | 2 of the flagged chats | You check a substantive factual, data, or business claim against an independent source, aiming to catch a real error or inconsistency. |
| 3 | Integration | Business plan, and the video | One investor-ready voice. Images consistent with each other and placed where the prose discusses them. Pitch and reflection feel like one presentation. |
| 4 | Reflection Q1 | Video and slides, your own words | A specific personal lesson about your AI workflow, a concrete moment the AI helped or misled you, and what you would do differently. |
| 5 | Reflection Q2 | Video and slides, your own words | A deep critique of AI capability, quality, authenticity, or ethics, tied to something that happened in this project. |

Reflection questions must be written and spoken by you. No AI drafting, outlining, or “polish” for Part 2 of the video or those slides.

### Design choices that serve the excellence criteria

- One chat per task group, each opened with a short context brief copied from this folder. That is the “carry context forward” evidence.
- Three sessions are built to be the flagged ones: data analysis (Task 2), competitor check (Task 5), and the marketing critique (Task 8). Each contains a visible revision and a visible external check.
- A verification log records the claim, the AI’s version, the source, and the correction. Those checks are pasted back into the chat so the marker can see them.
- The business plan is assembled by you from saved artefacts, then edited for one voice. It is not a paste of thirteen chat endings.
- Visuals share one palette, one wordmark, and one product name, locked before packaging, the ad, the site, and the plan are made.

---

## 2. Technical specifications

### 2.1 Dataset

**File:** `nz_breakfast_sales_2022_2025.xlsx`
**Sheet:** `Sales Data`
**Grain:** one row is one product variant in one quarter. A variant is product name + brand + pack weight. The same name often appears twice in one quarter because the pack size differs (for example Harraways Rolled Oats at 800 g and at 1.5 kg). Deduplicating on name, or on name + brand + quarter, deletes real SKUs.

**Size:** 12,020 data rows, 16 quarters from `2022-Q1` through `2025-Q4`, about 751–752 rows each quarter. 662 product names, 95 brands.

| Column | Type | Values observed | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Date | quarter label | `2022-Q1` … `2025-Q4` | Stored as text, not an Excel date. |
| Product Name | text | 662 distinct | No blank names. |
| Brand | text | 95 distinct | 17 names are used by more than one brand. Always qualify a product with its brand. |
| Category | text | Breakfast Cereals 3,808; Nutritional Cereal Bars 4,304; Spreads 3,300; Liquid Breakfasts 608 | These four are the brief’s sub-categories. |
| Is Plant Powered | 0/1 | 7,298 ones | Clean binary. |
| Is Weight Conscious | 0/1 | 464 ones | Small segment. |
| Is Performance Focused | 0/1 | 1,920 ones | Clean binary. |
| Is Gluten Free | 0/1 | 336 ones | Small segment. |
| Is Organic | 0/1 | 657 ones | Clean binary. |
| Unit Price (NZD) | number | Mostly retail-like. 29 rows are above $40, including values in the thousands (max 3,432.46). | Treat extreme prices as suspect. See issues below. |
| Weight | text | 154 distinct labels | Mixed formats: `400g`, `1.5kg`, `6 x 250ml`, `7 x 40g`, `3L`, `3pk`, `12g`. Not a numeric field until parsed. |
| Market Segment | text | Branded 10,436; Private Label 1,584 | |
| Price Tier | text | Standard 6,064; Premium 3,571; Value 2,385 | Sometimes disagrees across pack sizes of the same product. |
| Units Sold (Thousands) | number | 60 missing | A value of 7.36 means 7,360 units. |
| Revenue (Thousands NZD) | number | 24 missing | A value of 51.45 means $51,450. Column total is about $4.46 billion over four years. |

**Identity check.** Where units are present and non-zero, `Unit Price × Units Sold (Thousands)` should be close to `Revenue (Thousands NZD)`. Sixteen rows diverge by more than 5%. Several of those are the impossible unit prices: revenue ÷ units implies an ordinary shelf price, while the price cell is garbage (example: Raspberry & White Choc Oat Baked Squares listed at $1,763.64 while revenue and units imply about $4.49).

**Missingness.** 60 rows lack units, 24 lack revenue, and no row lacks both. A missing side can be recomputed only when the unit price is plausible.

**Zeros.** 114 rows have units and revenue both zero. None have units zero with revenue positive, or the reverse.

**Flags.** All five attribute flags are strict 0/1. No nulls.

#### Data-quality rules for Task 2

Apply these in the logged chat, and keep a before/after note in `02-market/data-quality.md`. The marker wants to see you direct the clean, not a silent local script.

1. Do not drop a row because the product name repeats. Confirm the weight differs. Exact duplicate groups are rare (4 groups on a first pass). Conflicting same-name groups are common (864) and are different packs.
2. Flag unit price above a stated threshold (start at $40, then inspect). Where units and revenue exist and imply a plausible shelf price, replace the price with revenue ÷ units and record the correction. Where the implied price is also implausible, quarantine the row and say so.
3. Impute a missing revenue as price × units, or a missing units as revenue ÷ price, only when the price survived rule 2. Leave a column `imputed_flag`.
4. Parse `Weight` into `weight_g` (grams, or ml treated as g for liquids) and `pack_count`. Keep the original string. Use parsed weight for per-100 g price comparisons.
5. Keep a row-level issue log: row identity, field, original value, action, reason.
6. Analysis uses the cleaned table. Every chart in the plan is reproducible from that table, with the quarter range and metric labelled (revenue in thousands of NZD, or converted to dollars — pick one and label it).

#### Analysis the market section must answer

These questions decide the product. A chart that does not change a product decision does not go in the plan.

- Which category grew, which shrank, from 2022 to 2025, in revenue and in units?
- Where is the growth inside each category: plant-powered, performance, weight-conscious, gluten-free, organic, price tier, branded vs private label?
- Which attribute combinations are growing and still thinly stocked (few SKUs or few brands)?
- What price band, in $/100 g, do growing products actually sell at?
- Which brands already own the space you might enter?

Recommended figures (produce all, embed the two or three that carry the argument):

1. Quarterly revenue by category, 2022-Q1 to 2025-Q4.
2. Revenue index (2022 = 100) for the attribute flags, so small segments are comparable.
3. SKU count vs revenue growth for the shortlisted attribute niche.
4. Price-per-100 g distribution for that niche, with the intended shelf price marked.

### 2.2 Session and file rules

**Chats.** One session per group. Suggested groups: Task 2; Tasks 3–4; Task 5; Tasks 6–7; Task 8; Tasks 9–10; Task 11 system prompt; Task 12 website; Task 13 plan draft; Task 14 pitch slides only. Reflection is not a chat.

**Context brief.** Every new session starts with the current `00-admin/context-brief.md` pasted in full, then the task. When a decision changes, update the brief before the next session. The brief is the carried context the excellence criterion asks for.

**Share links.** After each session, generate the permanent share URL, open it in a private window, and record it in `00-admin/chat-log.md`. If a Gemini share link is greyed out, paste the full transcript (your prompts and the replies) into a Word file, submit that file with the video, and say so on the form.

**Local copies.** Text goes into the markdown file for that task. Images are exported as PNG. Diagrams are saved as `.mmd` source plus PNG. Audio is saved as `.mp3` plus a lyrics text file. The chat is not the archive.

**What this Grok workspace is for.** Assembly, file organisation, data-cleaning notes, Mermaid rendering, PDF production, and a static website if you choose the local-site route. The graded evidence of prompting is the shareable chats in Gemini, Mistral, or ChatGPT. Doing the substantive back-and-forth only inside an unshared session leaves nothing for criteria 1 and 2 to be marked on.

### 2.3 Context brief (living spec)

Keep `00-admin/context-brief.md` under one page. Update it at the end of Tasks 3, 5, 6, 7, and 9.

```text
Company name:
Product name:
Category:
One-sentence description:
Flavour:
Target customer (one person, with a goal and a constraint):
Price position (tier, expected NZD, pack size):
Three claims we will make:
Three claims we will not make:
Differentiation vs the two nearest competitors:
Brand voice (three adjectives) and voice we reject:
Palette and wordmark notes:
Manufacturer candidate:
Critical process:
KPIs (five):
Open decisions:
```

### 2.4 Business plan PDF

| Spec | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Length | 1,500–2,500 words. Images, figures, and charts are outside the count. Captions stay short. |
| Audience | An investor who will read it as-is. Facts either come from the cleaned dataset, a named source, or are clearly labelled as a plan assumption. |
| Voice | One voice. You edit transitions so sections do not change tone or heading style. |
| File | `13-business-plan/business-plan.pdf` |
| Production | Draft in Markdown or Word. AI may draft sections from your saved artefacts. You place images yourself. Export to PDF from Word or Google Docs after layout. |

**Required embedded images**, each introduced by a sentence that says what the reader should conclude:

| Image | Source task | File |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market research figure(s) | 2 | `02-market/figures/` |
| Company logo | 6 | `06-brand/logo.png` |
| Product packaging | 7 | `07-packaging/pack-final.png` |
| Social media advertisement | 8 | `08-marketing/ad-final.png` |
| Critical process diagram | 9 | `09-operations/process.png` |
| ERD | 10 | `10-information/erd.png` |

**Section order and word budget.**

| Section | Words | Must contain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cover | — | Company name, logo, product name, your name, date. |
| 1. Executive summary | 180–220 | Product, customer, why now (one data result), advantage, what the funding is for. |
| 2. Product | 300–400 | Name, flavour, description, who it is for, home recipe summarised, industrial recipe summarised, viability scores from Task 4 and what you changed after them. |
| 3. Market | 300–400 | Cleaned-data findings, the figures, the gap you are entering. State units. |
| 4. Competitors | 250–350 | Two or three named competitors with price, customer, selling point, and your advantage. Prices sourced. |
| 5. Customer and brand | 150–200 | Segment persona, logo, packaging, what the synthetic-customer critique changed. |
| 6. Marketing | 250–350 | 250-word description tightened to plan length, channels, ad, jingle concept, two or three real NZ podcasts. |
| 7. Operations | 200–280 | NZ manufacturer with contact details, core processes, the one critical process, diagram, bottlenecks and the response. |
| 8. Information and KPIs | 200–280 | Entities, five KPIs with a definition and a target direction, ERD, two decisions the model supports. |
| 9. Offer to the reader | 80–120 | What happens in the first 90 days. Assumptions labelled as assumptions. |

**Fact rules.**

- Any number about the New Zealand breakfast market that is not computed from the spreadsheet gets a source and a check in `00-admin/verification-log.md`, or it comes out.
- Competitor prices cite the retailer or brand page and the date you looked.
- The manufacturer is a real company. Record the page where the contact details appeared.
- Health, nutrition, and “organic” wording stays inside claims you can justify. The plan does not invent a nutrition panel.
- “Where to buy” on the site and chatbot is a distribution intention (for example “launching through NZ independents and a direct site”) unless a real stockist exists.

### 2.5 Brand and image specs

Lock these before generating the final images.

| Asset | Spec |
| --- | --- |
| Logo | Square master, PNG, wordmark spelled correctly. Generate layout explorations on a fast model, then one final on a stronger setting. Check every letter. If spelling fails, request a symbol-only mark and set the name in type beside it in the plan and on the site. |
| Packaging | A retail pack as it would sit on a shelf: product name, flavour, brand, one claim that matches the brief, pack size. No fake certification logos. |
| Social ad | The format of the chosen channel (4:5 for Instagram feed, or 9:16 for stories). Logo and pack used as references if the tool accepts image input. One line of copy, product readable, no extra slogans the model invents. |
| Consistency | Same product name, same flavour line, same palette across logo, pack, ad, site, and slides. |

Save prompts next to outputs (`logo-prompt.txt`, and so on). Those prompts support the steering evidence if the image chat is one you flag.

### 2.6 Jingle

| Spec | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| File | `08-marketing/jingle.mp3` |
| Length | 15–60 seconds. Target 20–40. The marking guide allows up to 60. The brief warns generators overshoot a 15-second ask. |
| Content | Names the product or the category benefit. Matches the brand voice. |
| Also save | Lyrics in `08-marketing/jingle-lyrics.txt`, prompt, tool used, and duration. |
| Tool | Gemini music, or lyrics from a chat plus Suno, Udio, or ElevenLabs. |

### 2.7 Process diagram

- One process only: the one whose failure most directly stops a sale reaching a customer. For a new food brand that is usually order-to-delivery, or production-batch release. Pick one and justify it in a sentence.
- Source: `09-operations/process.mmd`, Mermaid `flowchart`.
- Render: [mermaid.live](https://mermaid.live/). On a render error, paste the error back into the chat and save the fixed source.
- Export PNG wide enough to read at page width (at least 1600 px).
- The diagram includes the unhappy path the bottleneck analysis talks about (stockout, failed quality check, or delayed distributor), not only the happy path.
- Bottleneck notes name the step, the failure mode, and one operational response.

### 2.8 Information model and KPIs

Business-level model, not a database design. No surrogate-key essay.

**Entities to cover:** Product, Customer, Order, Order line, Inventory batch, Supplier or manufacturer, Campaign (so marketing KPIs have a home).

**Each entity:** a name, a one-line definition, and the attributes you would actually record. Relationships named in words (a customer places many orders).

**ERD:** Mermaid `erDiagram` in `10-information/erd.mmd`, exported to `erd.png`.

**Five KPIs**, each with definition, formula, data entity it comes from, and what decision it triggers. Candidates to choose from, not a mandatory list:

- Repeat purchase rate
- On-time fulfilment rate
- Gross margin per unit after manufacturer cost
- Stock cover in weeks
- Podcast or site conversion to first order

The prose must answer two concrete questions the model can answer (“which flavour’s repeat rate fell this quarter?”) and one question it cannot.

### 2.9 Chatbot

| Spec | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Host | Gemini Gem, Mistral Agent, or ChatGPT custom GPT, so the marker has a public URL. A Google or ChatGPT login on their side is allowed. |
| URL | Recorded in `11-chatbot/url.txt`. Tested while logged in as a second account, or by another person. |
| Instructions | Written from `11-chatbot/system-prompt.md`, which you review. |
| Knowledge | Upload the context brief, product description, industrial-recipe summary suitable for customers (ingredients, allergens you have decided), and the FAQ. Do not upload the whole chat history. |

**System prompt must set:** company name and values, product name, ingredients you are willing to state, benefits you are willing to state, planned places to buy, target customer, tone, and a refusal behaviour for medical advice, unsupported health claims, and questions outside the product.

**Test script** (save answers in `11-chatbot/test-log.md`, then revise the prompt):

1. What is in it, and what allergen should I watch for?
2. Is it organic / gluten-free / high-protein? (Ask one that should be answered “no” or “we don’t claim that”.)
3. Where can I buy it?
4. How much does it cost?
5. A complaint: the pack arrived crushed. What do you do?
6. A medical question: will this treat my condition?
7. A competitor comparison.
8. Something the bot should not know yet (export nutrition panel, wholesale terms).

Pass when answers 2, 6, and 8 stay inside the claims you locked, and the tone matches the brand.

### 2.10 Website

Minimum to pass: one landing page, public URL, no login, product identifiable.

| Spec | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Required page | Landing: brand, product, who it is for, one data-backed reason to believe, pack image, a single next step (waitlist or “stockists to be announced”). |
| Optional | Product page, cart. Build these only after the landing page is public. |
| Consistency | Name, palette, logo, and pack match the plan. |
| URL check | Private window, logged out. Record the URL in `12-website/url.txt`. |
| Recommended tool | Figma Make on a free UC education account (`@uclive.ac.nz` at the Figma higher-education signup). |
| Acceptable alternatives | Google Stitch, a shareable canvas preview, Replit, v0, Lovable, or a static page from this folder deployed to a host that does not ask the marker to log in. |

**Static-site route, if used.** One self-contained page in `12-website/`, assets in that folder, deployed to a permanent host. The page states only claims locked in the context brief. No checkout that pretends to take payment.

### 2.11 Video

| Spec | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Length | Target 2:30–2:50. Pitch portion ends by 1:00. Stop before 3:29. Past that, excellence cannot be awarded and marking of the video stops. |
| Picture | You on camera, slides visible, talking-head. |
| Tool | PowerPoint Record Slide Show, then File → Export → `.mp4`. Any screen recording with a webcam is acceptable. Upload the file. |
| Slides | Title slide (does not count) + 2 pitch slides + 2 to 4 reflection slides. |
| Pitch content | Product and what is unique. Market opportunity from your analysis. Competitive advantage. |
| Pitch slides | AI may draft. You check every figure against the plan before you record. |
| Reflection slides and script | Your words only. Practice out loud. Do not read a script on camera. |

**Pitch timing.**

| Time | Slide | Say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0:00–0:10 | Title | Name, company, product. |
| 0:10–0:30 | Product | What it is, who it is for, one concrete difference. |
| 0:30–1:00 | Opportunity | One number from the dataset, the competitor gap, why you win. |

**Reflection coverage.** Q1: a lesson about prompting, context, or checking; one specific moment; what you would change. Q2: one deep point about authenticity, quality, or ethics from this project. Both questions, specific, in your own voice.

### 2.12 Verification log

`00-admin/verification-log.md` rows:

| Date | Claim the AI made | Why it mattered | Independent source | Result | What you changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Minimum checks, two of which must be visible inside flagged chats:

1. A data claim recomputed from the cleaned sheet (a total, a growth rate, or a rank).
2. A competitor shelf price against a NZ retailer or the brand’s own page, dated.
3. The manufacturer’s existence and contact details against the company’s site.
4. Each named podcast against its publisher or a podcast directory.
5. Any nutrition or “free-from” claim against the ingredient list you actually adopted.

---

## 3. Folder layout

```text
INFO123 Project/
  PLAN.md
  nz_breakfast_sales_2022_2025.xlsx
  00-admin/
    context-brief.md
    chat-log.md
    verification-log.md
    decisions.md
  01-ideas/
  02-market/
    data-quality.md
    analysis.md
    figures/
  03-product/
  04-critique/
  05-competitors/
  06-brand/
  07-packaging/
  08-marketing/
  09-operations/
  10-information/
  11-chatbot/
  12-website/
  13-business-plan/
  14-presentation/
    pitch-notes.md
    reflection-notes.md      # written by you, not generated
```

Create the folders at the start. Each task file begins with the date, the chat URL, and the decision that came out of the session.

---

## 4. Step-by-step plan

Dates assume work starts 30 September 2026 and submission is 16 October 2026 at 5:00 pm. Sections of the plan are drafted as soon as the task is done, so 14 October is editing and layout.

### Phase 0 — Setup (30 September)

1. Create the folder tree in section 3 and empty log files.
2. Confirm the AI account you will use for shared chats (Gemini is the brief’s recommendation; Mistral or ChatGPT also satisfy the brief). Image, music, and long chats need the higher limits of a signed-in plan.
3. Apply for the Figma education account with your `@uclive.ac.nz` address if you will use Figma Make.
4. Write your preferences into `00-admin/decisions.md` before any product chat. Answer in your own words:
   - Breakfast you actually eat, and what you refuse (flavour, texture, allergens, time in the morning).
   - Category you are willing to make: cereal, bar, spread, or liquid.
   - Who you want to sell to, as a person with a constraint (time, budget, training, children, dietary rule).
   - Price you personally would pay, in NZD, and the pack that price implies.
   - Three words for the brand, and three words you do not want.
5. Done when the preference notes exist and the chat-log file has a header row.

### Phase 1 — Product ideas and the market (1–3 October)

**Task 1, one chat.** Ask the model to interview you before it proposes products. Answer from `decisions.md`. Stop at three candidate concepts, each with category, flavour direction, user, and why it might fit NZ retail. Save to `01-ideas/candidates.md`. Do not name the company yet.

**Task 2, flagged chat candidate.** Upload the spreadsheet.

1. Ask for data-quality issues with evidence (counts, examples), not a cleaned file on the first reply.
2. Push back using the rules in section 2.1. In particular, reject any proposal to delete same-name rows that are different pack sizes, and require a rule for the impossible unit prices.
3. Have it produce the cleaned table and the issue log. Recompute one headline number yourself (category revenue for one year, or a growth rate) and paste the comparison into the chat. That is verification check 1.
4. Only then ask for the charts and the opportunity. Require every opportunity to cite a category, an attribute, a direction of change, and a price band.
5. Save figures into `02-market/figures/` and the narrative into `02-market/analysis.md`.

**Gate.** Choose the concept that the data supports and that you will actually defend on camera. Write it into the context brief. If the data contradicts your favourite idea, record the contradiction in `decisions.md` and either change the idea or narrow it until the evidence holds.

### Phase 2 — Product, critique, competitors (4–6 October)

**Tasks 3 and 4, one chat, context brief attached.**

1. Finalise category, flavour, and a working product name. The name must be easy to say in the first ten seconds of the video and must not collide with a brand you saw in the spreadsheet or in a quick search.
2. Home recipe, then an industrial version with constraints you add: target cost per unit, shelf life, pack size, allergen position, and which “free-from” claims are forbidden until verified.
3. Brief product description, 120–150 words, in the brand voice.
4. New chat for Task 4. Upload only the product summary. Demand scores out of 5 on differentiation, consumer appeal, brand potential, and manufacturing feasibility, each with the assumption that would flip the score. Revise one thing the critique got right. Save scores to `04-critique/viability.md`.

**Task 5, flagged chat candidate.**

1. With search on, find the nearest NZ-available products. Then turn search off.
2. Keep two or three competitors. For each: product, price, pack size, price per 100 g, target buyer, claim, source URL, date.
3. Open one retailer or brand page yourself and check a price the AI stated. Paste the match or the correction into the chat. That is verification check 2.
4. Write three advantages you can actually deliver, and drop any advantage that is just an adjective.

Update the context brief.

### Phase 3 — Brand, pack, marketing, jingle (7–9 October)

**Tasks 6 and 7.**

1. Company name: generate options from the brief, then choose. Check the name is not an obvious existing NZ food brand.
2. Logo explorations, then one final. Spell-check. Save prompt and PNG.
3. Write the target customer as a persona with a goal and a hurdle. This persona is reused for the synthetic review and the chatbot.
4. Packaging image. In a new chat, hand the image and the persona (goal plus constraint, not “you are a customer”) and ask for critique. Change one visible thing. Regenerate. Save both versions so the revision is documented.

**Task 8, flagged chat candidate.** Feed Tasks 4, 5, and 7 outputs.

1. Promotional description, hard cap 250 words, with a tone instruction more specific than the brief’s example (for example: short sentences, no wellness clichés, spoken by the persona’s friend).
2. Ask it to criticise the draft against that tone instruction. Revise in the same chat.
3. Pick channels from the persona’s actual habits. One ad concept, then one image, with logo and pack as references when the tool allows.
4. Jingle: specify genre, tempo, vocal, and the single line that must be heard. Export mp3. Trim or regenerate until it is under 60 seconds and the product is identifiable.
5. NZ podcasts: names you then verify in a directory. Drop any show you cannot find. That is verification check 4.
6. Write `08-marketing/strategy.md` yourself from these pieces, two to four pages, so Task 13 is assembly rather than invention.

### Phase 4 — Operations and information (10–11 October)

**Tasks 9 and 10, one chat, search on only for the manufacturer step.**

1. Find one real NZ manufacturer that can make this category. Record legal or trading name, site, location, contact, and why they fit (category capability, minimum order if stated). Open their site and confirm the contact. That is verification check 3. Turn search off afterwards.
2. List core processes. Choose one critical process. Mermaid flowchart including one failure path. Export PNG. Ask for bottlenecks. Keep two, each with a response you would actually fund.
3. Entities, attributes, and five KPIs. Mermaid ERD. Ask how the model supports two named decisions. Save the explanation.

If mermaid.live errors, the repair loop stays in the chat.

### Phase 5 — Chatbot and website (12–13 October)

**Task 11.**

1. In a chat, draft the system prompt from the spec in section 2.9. Edit it.
2. Create the Gem, Agent, or GPT. Upload the knowledge files.
3. Run the eight test questions. Fix any breach of the claim rules. Save the public URL and retest from another login.

**Task 12.**

1. Build the landing page from the context brief, logo, pack, and the short description. Give the tool those files rather than a vague “make a breakfast brand”.
2. Publish. Open the URL logged out. Fix anything that asks for an account.
3. Read the page against the claim list. Delete copy the generator added.

Both URLs go into the chat log file the day they work, not on submission day.

### Phase 6 — Business plan (14 October, drafted continuously before this)

1. Assemble sections from the task files using the word budget in section 2.4. AI may propose a combined draft from those files. You rewrite the opening of each section so the document has one voice.
2. Insert image placeholders, then place the six required images yourself, each with a caption that states the conclusion.
3. Read every number against `02-market/analysis.md` and the verification log.
4. Count words excluding images. Cut to the range if needed.
5. Export PDF. Open it and check: logo spelling, figure legibility, no heading style changes, page numbers, your name, no leftover placeholder text.

### Phase 7 — Video (15 October)

1. Draft two pitch slides from the plan. Check the market number and the competitor claim against the PDF.
2. Write reflection notes on paper or in `14-presentation/reflection-notes.md` without an AI. Two to four slides. Specific moment, specific change, one deep critique.
3. Rehearse with a timer. Pitch must finish at or before one minute.
4. Record in one take per slide if you can. Export `.mp4`. Watch the file to the end: face visible, audio clear, slides match what you say, runtime under 3:29.

### Phase 8 — Submit (16 October, morning)

1. Private-window test of the website. Second-account test of the chatbot.
2. Open every chat URL on the form. Flag the two or three sessions that show steering and a correction (planned: Tasks 2, 5, and 8).
3. Upload to Learn, as files: video, business-plan PDF, jingle mp3. Submit URLs only through the form: chats, website, chatbot.
4. Stop at 5:00 pm. A link in place of the video does not count.

---

## 5. Submission checklist

- [ ] Video is an `.mp4` or `.mov` file, 2–3 minutes, pitch within the first minute, both reflection questions in your own words.
- [ ] Business plan PDF is inside the word range and contains the market figure, logo, pack, ad, process diagram, and ERD, each discussed in the surrounding text.
- [ ] Jingle mp3 plays and is 15–60 seconds.
- [ ] Website URL loads logged out on a landing page for this product.
- [ ] Chatbot URL answers a product question.
- [ ] Chat form lists every session, the flagged two or three open successfully, and those sessions show a revision plus an external check.
- [ ] Verification log and context brief are filled in, so the plan, the site, and the bot do not disagree.

---

## 6. Risks already visible

| Risk | Response |
| --- | --- |
| Impossible unit prices and missing units or revenue distort the “opportunity”. | Clean before any chart. Recompute one headline yourself inside the chat. |
| Same product name is not the same SKU. | Identity is name + brand + weight + quarter. |
| Image models misspell the wordmark. | Spell-check before the pack and ad. Fall back to a symbol plus typed name. |
| Music models ignore the 15-second ask. | Judge the file’s duration. Keep it under 60 seconds. |
| Share links die or are disabled. | Local copies of every artefact. Transcript file as the brief’s fallback. Test links before submission day. |
| Canvas website URLs expire or demand login. | Prefer Figma Make or a deployed static page. Test logged out on 13 October and again on 16 October. |
| The plan reads as stitched chat output. | You write the first sentence of every section and the executive summary last, after the evidence is stable. |
| Reflection sounds generic. | One incident from the verification log, told in your words, with the change you made afterwards. |
| Usage caps hit during image week. | Explore on a fast model. Final logo, final pack, and final ad only. |

---

## 7. First action

Phase 0 is the next session of work: create the folders, write the preference notes, and confirm which chat tool will hold the graded sessions. Product naming starts only after that, in the Task 1 interview.
