# STAMP

## Executive summary

Stamp is a sheet of peel-and-press spreads for toast. Each stamp is a 10 g disc on a food-safe release film, nested in a printed card. You peel one off and press it onto hot toast. The heat softens it into a layer. There is no knife and no open jar. An unopened sheet is made to keep for 12 months in a pantry. The home recipes that test flavour are not that product. They stay in the fridge and are eaten within 7 days.

The buyer is someone who eats toast away from a full kitchen. That might be a flat, an office, a hall, or a bag. They want a decided portion of flavour without carrying a jar or washing a knife.

Cleaned New Zealand breakfast sales put spreads revenue at about $275 million NZD in 2022 and about $341 million NZD in 2025. That is about 24% growth. Premium spreads grew faster than value spreads, from about $88 million NZD to about $113 million NZD, while value moved only from about $36 million NZD to about $39 million NZD. The category got larger, and the growth was not confined to the cheapest jars.

A jar is a shared tub. It needs a knife and somewhere to set the open pack. A stamp is one portion, already the right size, and it travels in a sheet. The sheet is $5.00 NZD for 80 g, which is $6.25 NZD per 100 g. That sits above the 90th percentile of branded spreads in the cleaned file, $5.19 NZD per 100 g. The gap is the film and the card, which a jar does not carry. None of the 154 spread names describes a portion or a peel-and-press product. Stamp is a different format, not another jar.

## Product

The launch line is four flavours: Salted Butter, Raspberry, Yeast extract, and Peanut. A single-flavour sheet holds eight stamps of one flavour. A mixed sheet holds two of each. Every sheet is 80 g net and $5.00 NZD on the shelf, so every sheet is $6.25 NZD per 100 g. One stamp is 10 g, about $0.63 NZD of that shelf price.

Salted Butter is a shelf-stable butter spread, not a pat of fridge butter. The word butter on its own is a dairy-identity standard in Australia and New Zealand, so the sheet shows the flavour name and then the word spread. The sold disc is cultured butterfat and salt, in the same ratio as the home batch: 2 g of salt to 78 g of fat. No oil is added. Moisture is kept low enough that the sealed disc stays stable in a pantry and still softens on hot toast. The stamp contains milk. The home prototype is softened unsalted butter beaten with that salt, pressed onto baking paper, and eaten from the fridge within 7 days. It tests the flavour and the gesture. It is not what we sell.

Raspberry is fruit, sugar, and lemon, cooked down. The home batch starts with 120 g of raspberries, 30 g of caster sugar, and 5 g of lemon juice, and it is stirred until 80 g of thick paste remains. The industrial disc uses that same cook, deposited at 10 g. The label says it is made with 150 g of raspberries per 100 g because 120 g of fruit was reduced to 80 g. The paste holds its shape from the solids in the cook and from the seal, not from a preservative claim. The recipe itself names no major allergen. The sheet still carries the facility line.

Yeast extract is our own paste. It is not Marmite and it is not Vegemite, and those names do not appear on the pack. The home prototype warms 55 g of yeast extract with 15 g of tomato paste, 8 g of black treacle, and 2 g of salt until it holds a disc. The sold formula is the one on the label: yeast extract 80%, barley malt extract 15.5%, salt 2.5%, and vegetable concentrate 2%. The salt share matches the home batch. Barley malt extract means the stamp contains gluten from barley.

Peanut contains peanuts. The home paste is 85 g of roasted peanuts and 1.5 g of fine salt, ground until firm and portioned before the oil separates. The sold disc is roasted peanuts 96%, vegetable fat 2.3% as a hard-fat stabiliser, and salt 1.7%. The stabiliser is there so the disc does not oil off across 12 months.

Every sheet, including Raspberry and the mixed sheet, is made in a facility that handles milk and peanuts. The mixed sheet contains milk, gluten, and peanuts because it contains all four flavours. Nutrition figures on the pack backs are calculated from these proportions and from published composition figures. They are not a laboratory assay, and this plan does not treat them as tested results. The pack carries no certification mark.

The making step is the same shape for every flavour. Deposit 10 g, give or take 0.5 g, onto release film. Cut the disc. Nest eight discs in the card. Flow-wrap the sheet. If the weight check fails, or the film will not release, that stamp is rejected. It does not ship inside a sheet that looks finished. Only the sealed, unopened sheet claims 12 months at ambient temperature.

Use is four moves. Keep the sheet in a pantry. Peel a stamp off the release film. Press it onto hot toast. Wait a few seconds so the residual heat lays the spread across the slice.

## Market

The figures here come from the cleaned sales file, not from the raw spreadsheet totals. Money is in million NZD. The source column was stored in thousands of NZD, and it has been scaled so the unit is written out.

Spreads revenue was about $275 million NZD in 2022, about $305 million NZD in 2023, about $319 million NZD in 2024, and about $341 million NZD in 2025. From 2022 to 2025 that is about 24% growth. The 2024 total sits a little above the raw column because blank revenue cells in that year were filled during cleaning. Other years barely moved. Unit volume, counted here in millions of units rather than in the source's thousands, rose from about 32.8 million in 2022 to about 40.2 million in 2025. Revenue grew slightly faster than the number of units, so the category was not only moving more packs at a flat price.

The tier split is the sharper reading. Value spreads moved from about $36 million NZD to about $39 million NZD. Premium moved from about $88 million NZD to about $113 million NZD. Standard, still the largest tier, moved from about $151 million NZD to about $189 million NZD. Premium's rate of growth was faster than value's. Standard added the most dollars. A new sheet priced like a value jar would be walking into the slow part of the category. A sheet priced above ordinary jars is at least pointed at a tier that grew. It is not pointed at the bulk of the money, which is still standard jars. That is the limit on what the bars can justify.

:::figure

Price per 100 g, for branded spreads, says where $6.25 sits. The far tail is manuka honey, not peanut butter or jam. Fix & Fogg's SKU medians in the cleaned file sit around $2.65 NZD per 100 g. caption: At $6.25 NZD per 100 g, the Stamp sheet sits to the right of almost every branded spread in this chart.

# STAMP

## Executive summary

Stamp is a peel-and-press spread for toast. Each stamp is a 10 g disc on food-safe release film, nested in a printed card. You peel it off and press it onto hot toast, and the heat softens it into a layer. There is no knife and no open jar. An unopened sheet is made to keep for 12 months in a pantry. Home batches that test flavour are eaten from the fridge within 7 days. They are not the product we sell.

The buyer eats toast away from a full kitchen: a flat, an office, a hall, or a bag. They want one decided portion, not a jar to carry and a knife to wash.

Cleaned New Zealand breakfast sales put spreads revenue at about $275 million NZD in 2022 and about $341 million NZD in 2025. That is about 24% growth. Premium grew faster than value, from about $88 million NZD to about $113 million NZD, while value moved from about $36 million NZD to about $39 million NZD.

A jar is a shared tub. A stamp is one portion in a sheet. The sheet is $5.00 NZD for 80 g, which is $6.25 NZD per 100 g, above the 90th percentile of branded spreads in the cleaned file ($5.19 NZD per 100 g). The extra is the film and the card. None of the 154 spread names describes a portion or a peel-and-press product. The opening is the format, not another jar.

## Product

Four flavours launch together: Salted Butter, Raspberry, Yeast extract, and Peanut. A single-flavour sheet holds eight stamps. A mixed sheet holds two of each. Every sheet is 80 g and $5.00 NZD, so $6.25 NZD per 100 g. One stamp is about $0.63 NZD of the shelf price.

Salted Butter is a shelf-stable butter spread, not a pat of fridge butter. The sheet prints the flavour name and then the word spread, because butter on its own is a dairy-identity standard in Australia and New Zealand. The sold disc is cultured butterfat and salt, 2 g of salt to 78 g of fat, with no added oil. It contains milk. The home batch uses that same salt ratio in softened unsalted butter, then it is chilled and eaten within 7 days. Only the sealed industrial disc claims the pantry life.

Raspberry is raspberries, caster sugar, and lemon juice cooked to a thick paste. The home batch reduces 120 g of fruit, 30 g of sugar, and 5 g of lemon juice to 80 g. The sold disc is that paste, deposited at 10 g. The label says 150 g of raspberries per 100 g because of that reduction. The recipe names no major allergen of its own.

Yeast extract is our paste. It is not Marmite and it is not Vegemite, and those names are not on the pack. The home batch warms yeast extract with tomato paste, black treacle, and salt until it holds a disc. The sold formula is yeast extract 80%, barley malt extract 15.5%, salt 2.5%, and vegetable concentrate 2%. It contains gluten from barley.

Peanut contains peanuts. The home paste is roasted peanuts and salt, ground and portioned before the oil separates. The sold disc is roasted peanuts 96%, vegetable fat 2.3% so the oil does not separate over 12 months, and salt 1.7%.

Every sheet, including Raspberry, is made in a facility that handles milk and peanuts. The mixed sheet contains milk, gluten, and peanuts. Nutrition figures on the backs are calculated from these proportions and from published composition tables. They are not a laboratory assay, and this plan does not present them as tested. No certification mark is used.

Making is the same shape for each flavour. Deposit 10 g, give or take 0.5 g, onto release film, cut the disc, nest eight in the card, and flow-wrap. A failed weight check, or a film that will not release, is a rejected stamp, not a sheet that ships. To use one, keep the sheet in a pantry, peel a stamp, press it onto hot toast, and wait a few seconds.

Value spreads moved from about $36 million NZD to about $39 million. Premium moved from about $88 million to about $113 million. Standard, still the largest tier, moved from about $151 million to about $189 million. Premium's rate of growth was faster than value's. Standard added the most dollars. A sheet priced like a value jar would be aimed at the slow part of the category. Stamp is priced above ordinary jars, toward a tier that grew, and away from where most of the money still sits.

items.content: The product section is 411 words. It needs to be cut by more than 11 words to reach the 400-word limit.

Page 2 looks dense but readable.

Page 3 chart looks good. The price paragraph splits before the next chart. That is acceptable. Page 4 is next.

Page 2 text may clip the footer. I will check pages 4 through 6 first. The product section is 11 words over. I will trim about fifteen by shortening the last paragraph and the salt-ratio description.

A zero-width space in the URLs is rendering as a visible box. The zero-width space is invisible in the source but renders as a black box in reportlab because the font lacks that glyph. I will replace it with a regular break or normal space so URLs wrap cleanly without drawing a visible rectangle. I will insert explicit `
` tags after slashes in the URLs so they wrap cleanly without a visible glyph. I am also considering replacing slashes with slash-space to force wrapping at spaces. I will write a `break_url` helper that inserts `
` at slashes, question marks, or ampersands to wrap long URLs cleanly. This avoids the zero-width space entirely. I will modify the `soften()` regex callback to insert `
` tags after slashes in URLs. This replaces the zero-width space that was previously inserted into every URL. The URL splitting logic is being implemented. It splits each URL on slashes and rebuilds the string with `
` tags whenever a line would exceed 64 characters. The regex callback is safe because these URLs use `%27` instead of `&`. The marketing paragraph currently runs three URLs into one line, causing text to collide. Each podcast URL will be placed in its own paragraph so the link sits on the line after the description. This also fixes words like "ninetonoon" running together. Blank lines must be inserted between the podcast descriptions so each show sits in its own paragraph. The sentence about a show not taking the spot also needs to be separated into its own paragraph. Page 5 currently has a large empty region because the pack and ad row jumped to page 6. I will reduce the image row max height so the pack and ad fit on page 5 with the paragraph. A CondPageBreak before the pack paragraph will keep it with the images. The row is roughly 360 points tall, so reducing its max height to about 200 points should let it fit on page 5. The pack paragraph is orphaned from the images on page 5. I will move the entire pack block to page 6 by inserting a larger CondPageBreak before it. Page 5 will end after the logo, and page 6 will start with the pack sentence and images together. I will keep the last prose paragraph with its following figure or image row using KeepTogether. The paragraph is held back until the next block is a figure or row, then both are emitted together. This keeps the pack sentence and images on page 6 while page 5 ends after the logo caption. I will cap the image row height at 280 points so the paragraph and row together stay under 680 points and fit inside the 742-point frame. I will also cut one sentence from Product 411 to bring it under the word limit. The price paragraph and figure 03 will be kept together so the chart and its description stay on page 4. Page 3 will end with the tier chart and caption. I will also verify the PDF contains no remaining .notdef boxes. A visual check of the rendered PDF will confirm the zero-width space is gone. The competitor page will be re-read after the fix. Page 2 spacing and logo caption alignment look correct. The logo caption is left-aligned under the centered image, but its width matches the image so it appears centered. The pack and ad row looks correct with visible rounded corners and no clipping. The ad caption is one line while the pack caption wraps to two lines, but this mismatch is acceptable since the description does not require alignment. The zero-width space in URLs remains the primary defect; it also breaks the visual appearance of `https:// / www`. I removed fifteen words from Product, cutting "One stamp is about $0.63 NZD of the shelf price." and "until it holds a disc," which brings the total down to 396 words and satisfies the 300–400 band. The apostrophe in "buyer's" rendered correctly. CondPageBreak(88) will place the competitors section on page 4 and the customer section on page 5. The KeepTogether fix for the price chart’s introductory sentence is confirmed. I am now drafting an `emit_prose` helper that splits text into paragraphs and holds the last paragraph back when a figure or row follows. The `emit_prose` helper is being drafted. It queues the last paragraph of a prose block and emits all earlier parts immediately. When a figure or row follows, the queued paragraph and the image flowables are wrapped in KeepTogether. The pending paragraph must be reset at section boundaries to avoid leaking across pages. I will test KeepTogether to avoid layout errors. I am checking whether the other workers have finished their files. The `
` tags are injected only during PDF rendering, so word counts remain accurate. I am also inspecting the visible boxes more carefully. The visible box is the .notdef glyph for U+200B. I will remove it from xml_text. The podcast copy is being restructured so each show description and URL sits in its own paragraph. The Front Page and Nine to Noon podcast descriptions are drafted with their URLs. The marketing section is now 230 words, so it still needs 20–120 more to reach the 250–350 target. The marketing section will gain roughly 20 words from the podcast restructure and another 50–70 from the jingle paragraph, landing near 300–320 words. The product cut is confirmed at exactly 15 words. Page 2 spacing looks tight but acceptable. Heading spaceBefore will be increased so sections do not crowd together on the same page. The code and draft will be updated, then preview pages for competitors URLs and customer page breaks will be re-rendered. Caption conclusions are already present. The logo on page 5 is the actual logo.png, not an empty box. Captions under images and chart captions will be centered using a new `cap` style with `TA_CENTER`. KeepTogether is already imported. Caption alignment under figures and image rows is confirmed correct. items.output:
1→# Sheet making and release

Figure: `diagrams/process.png`, from `diagrams/process.mmd`.

The pass path is order in, batch deposit onto film, cut, nest, check, pack, dispatch. At the check, a stamp outside 10 g ± 0.5 g, or a film that will not release, goes to Reject. That path stops. It does not join Pack or Dispatch, and the stamp does not ship.

## Bottlenecks

**1. Deposit weight.** Peanut paste and yeast extract thicken or slacken while they sit in the hopper, so the depositor drifts outside 10 g ± 0.5 g and the check rejects a run of discs.
10→
Response: stop the depositor. Weigh the next five discs. Restart only when all five sit between 9.5 g and 10.5 g. Discs that failed are rejected and are not nested.

**2. Release film.** A roll that will not peel fails only after spread is already on it, so one bad roll can reject a whole deposit run before pack.

Response: peel-test the first eight discs of each new roll. If one will not release, stop, quarantine that roll, and reject every stamp already on it. Load a fresh roll and test eight more before nesting continues. Nothing from the failed roll is packed or dispatched.

1→# Information notes

Entities in `diagrams/erd.mmd`: Customer, Order, OrderLine (the order line), Sheet (the sellable pack), Product (the flavour), Batch, Manufacturer, Campaign.

A Sheet includes one Product when the pack is a single flavour (8 stamps). The mixed sheet includes all four Products, two stamps of each. A Batch deposits one Product. A Batch supplies a Sheet only when the stamps passed the check. A Batch with release_rejects above zero failed release and those stamps are not on a dispatched Sheet.

## KPIs

**1. Repeat purchase rate.** Entity: Customer, counted from Order.
10→
Formula: number of Customers with two or more Orders, divided by the number of Customers with at least one Order.

**2. Stamps per order.** Entity: OrderLine, using Sheet.

Formula: sum of (OrderLine.sheet_qty times Sheet.stamps_on_sheet) across all order lines, divided by the number of Orders. stamps_on_sheet is 8 on every pack, including mixed.

**3. On-time dispatch rate.** Entity: Order.

Formula: number of Orders whose dispatched_on is on or before promised_dispatch, divided by the number of Orders that have a dispatched_on. An order with no dispatch date is not in this rate.
20→
**4. Batch rejection rate.** Entity: Batch.

Formula: (sum of weight_rejects + sum of release_rejects) divided by sum of stamps_checked. A weight reject is a stamp outside 10 g ± 0.5 g. A release reject is a stamp whose film will not release. Each checked stamp is counted once, under the first failure found. Rejected stamps are not packed and are not dispatched.

**5. Gross margin per sheet after manufacturer cost.** Entity: Sheet, for the shelf price. The cost term is an assumption, not a figure stored on Manufacturer, and not a quote from Griffiths & Co.

Formula, labelled as an assumption: shelf price $5.00, retailer share 35% ($1.75), so Stamp receives $5.00 times (1 minus 0.35) = $3.25. Subtract the assumed manufactured cost of $1.50. Gross margin per sheet = $3.25 minus $1.50 = $1.75. Change the 35% or the $1.50 and this margin changes. The recipes do not.

## Questions this model can answer
30→
Which flavour is reordered? A flavour is a Product. Follow Customer to Order to OrderLine to Sheet to Product. A reorder of a flavour is a later Order from the same Customer for a single-flavour Sheet whose only included Product is that flavour. A mixed Sheet is a separate pack (two of each), not a reorder of one flavour.

Which batch failed release? Read Batch.release_rejects. Any Batch with release_rejects above zero failed the film-release check. Those stamps do not supply a Sheet and do not go to dispatch. Manufacturer says who ran that batch.

## Question this model cannot answer

Whether a flavour has a medical effect. No entity records a symptom, a diagnosis, a test result, or any health outcome. Orders, batches, and flavours cannot support that claim, and the product does not make it.

items.output: 1→--- name: pdf description: Read, create, and transform PDF files. Covers pulling text and tables out of PDFs, generating new PDFs, merging and splitting documents, rotating pages, watermarking, encrypting or removing passwords, extracting embedded images, running OCR on scanned documents, and filling out PDF forms including official tax forms. Apply this skill whenever a task involves a .pdf file as input or deliverable. user-invocable: false --- # Working with PDFs Task-oriented recipes for PDF work, built around three Python libraries (`pypdf`, `pdfplumber`, `reportlab`) and the poppler-utils / qpdf command-line suites. 10→ Companion documents in this directory — open them when the task calls for it: - `forms.md` — required reading before filling out any PDF form - `tax.md` — required reading before preparing the official tax forms bundled under `forms/` - `reference.md` — deeper material: pypdfium2 rendering, JavaScript libraries (pdf-lib, pdfjs-dist), advanced qpdf/poppler flags, performance tuning, and troubleshooting ## Choosing a Tool | Goal | Reach for | 20→|------|-----------| | Pull out plain text | `pdfplumber` or `pdftotext` | | Pull out tables | `pdfplumber` (`extract_tables`) | | Combine documents | `pypdf` or `qpdf` | | Break a document apart | `pypdf` (one writer per output) | | Produce a new PDF | `reportlab` (Canvas for absolute layout, Platypus for flowing documents) | | Grab embedded images | `pdfimages` | | Render pages as pictures | `pdftoppm` / `pdf2image` | | OCR a scanned document | `pytesseract` + `pdf2image` | | Fill out a form | see `forms.md` | 30→ ## Getting Content Out of a PDF ### Text ```python import pdfplumber with pdfplumber.open("report.pdf") as doc: full_text = "\n".join(pg.extract_text() or "" for pg in doc.pages) 40→``` From the shell, `pdftotext` is quickest; `-layout` keeps the visual column structure and `-f`/`-l` bound the page range: ```bash pdftotext -layout report.pdf report.txt pdftotext -f 2 -l 4 report.pdf middle_pages.txt ``` ### Tables 50→ `pdfplumber` returns each table as a list of rows; feed them straight into pandas when you need to reshape or export: ```python import pandas as pd import pdfplumber frames = [] with pdfplumber.open("report.pdf") as doc: for pg in doc.pages: 60→ for tbl in pg.extract_tables(): if tbl: frames.append(pd.DataFrame(tbl[1:], columns=tbl[0])) if frames: pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True).to_excel("tables.xlsx", index=False) ``` ### Document Metadata 70→```python from pypdf import PdfReader info = PdfReader("report.pdf").metadata for key in ("title", "author", "subject", "creator"): print(key, "=", getattr(info, key)) ``` ### Embedded Images vs. Page Renders 80→These are different operations — pick the right one: - `pdfimages -all report.pdf img/fig` copies the *original bitmap objects* embedded in the file, untouched by page layout. - `pdftoppm -png -r 300 report.pdf pages/pg` *rasterizes* whole pages — text, vectors, and annotations included — producing what is effectively a screenshot of each page. A rendered page is never a substitute for an extracted image, and vice versa. ### Scanned Documents (OCR) Scanned PDFs contain pictures of text, so extraction tools return nothing useful. Rasterize first, then OCR each page: 90→ ```python # pip install pytesseract pdf2image import pytesseract from pdf2image import convert_from_path pages = convert_from_path("scan.pdf") recognized = [pytesseract.image_to_string(img) for img in pages] print("\n\n".join(recognized)) ``` 100→ ## Reorganizing Pages ### Combine Documents ```python from pypdf import PdfWriter writer = PdfWriter() for path in ["intro.pdf", "body.pdf", "appendix.pdf"]: 110→ writer.append(path) with open("combined.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` Or from the shell: ```bash qpdf --empty --pages intro.pdf body.pdf appendix.pdf -- combined.pdf 120→``` ### Split into Pieces ```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter src = PdfReader("combined.pdf") for idx, pg in enumerate(src.pages, start=1): part = PdfWriter() 130→ part.add_page(pg) with open(f"part_{idx}.pdf", "wb") as out: part.write(out) ``` `qpdf` handles page ranges without any code: ```bash qpdf combined.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- first_five.pdf ``` 140→ ### Rotate ```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter src = PdfReader("sideways.pdf") writer = PdfWriter() for pg in src.pages: writer.add_page(pg) 150→writer.pages[0].rotate(90) # clockwise degrees; must be a multiple of 90 with open("upright.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` ### Stamp a Watermark Overlay one PDF page (the watermark) onto every page of another: 160→```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter stamp = PdfReader("stamp.pdf").pages[0] src = PdfReader("contract.pdf") writer = PdfWriter() for pg in src.pages: pg.merge_page(stamp) writer.add_page(pg) 170→ with open("stamped.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` ### Passwords ```python from pypdf import PdfWriter 180→writer = PdfWriter() writer.append("private.pdf") writer.encrypt(user_password="open-me", owner_password="admin-key") with open("locked.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` Removing a known password is a one-liner: 190→```bash qpdf --password=open-me --decrypt locked.pdf unlocked.pdf ``` ## Generating PDFs with reportlab Two APIs, two mindsets: - **Canvas** — you place every element at explicit coordinates. The origin is the *bottom-left* corner of the page and y grows upward, so "1 inch from the top" is `page_height - inch - element_height`. - **Platypus** — you build a `story` list of flowables (`Paragraph`, `Table`, `Image`, `Spacer`, `PageBreak`) and the layout engine paginates for you. Prefer this for anything document-like. 200→ ### Minimal Examples ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas c = canvas.Canvas("note.pdf", pagesize=letter) _, page_h = letter c.drawString(72, page_h - 72, "Placed one inch from the top-left corner.") 210→c.line(72, page_h - 90, 400, page_h - 90) c.save() ``` ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet from reportlab.platypus import PageBreak, Paragraph, SimpleDocTemplate, Spacer styles = getSampleStyleSheet() 220→story = [ Paragraph("Annual Summary", styles["Title"]), Spacer(1, 12), Paragraph("Body text flows and wraps automatically. " * 15, styles["Normal"]), PageBreak(), Paragraph("Second Section", styles["Heading1"]), ] SimpleDocTemplate("summary.pdf", pagesize=letter).build(story) ``` 230→### Placing Images Keep the aspect ratio: derive the missing dimension from the source image, or let reportlab do it when fitting a box. ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.units import inch from reportlab.lib.utils import ImageReader from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas 240→c = canvas.Canvas("figure.pdf", pagesize=letter) _, page_h = letter src = ImageReader("chart.png") src_w, src_h = src.getSize() w = 4.5 * inch h = w * src_h / src_w # bottom-left origin: subtract the image height to hang it below the top margin c.drawImage(src, inch, page_h - inch - h, width=w, height=h) 250→c.save() ``` To fit an image inside a fixed region without distortion: ```python c.drawImage("photo.jpg", box_x, box_y, width=box_w, height=box_h, preserveAspectRatio=True, anchor="c") ``` 260→In Platypus, images are flowables — size them yourself and let the engine position them: ```python from reportlab.platypus import Image pic = Image("logo.png", width=w, height=h, hAlign="CENTER") story.append(pic) ``` Prefer `drawImage` over `drawInlineImage`; it registers the image once as a shared object, so repeated use is smaller and faster. 270→ ### Subscripts and Superscripts Do **not** type Unicode sub/superscript characters (₂, ⁹, …) — reportlab's built-in fonts lack those glyphs and they render as black rectangles. Use inline markup inside a `Paragraph` instead: ```python Paragraph("H2O and E = mc2", styles["Normal"]) ``` When drawing directly on a Canvas (no `Paragraph`), simulate the effect by shrinking the font and shifting the baseline manually. 280→ ### Tables Two non-negotiable rules, both consequences of how `Table` lays out cells: 1. **Every cell — headers included — goes inside a `Paragraph`.** Bare strings never wrap; long values run over neighboring cells or off the page. `Paragraph` cells also accept inline markup (``, ``, ``, ``). 2. **Pass explicit `colWidths`, sized by content.** Equal-width columns squeeze prose and waste space on short IDs. Budget most of the printable width (letter with 1" margins ≈ 6.5", landscape ≈ 9") to the prose-heavy columns. ```python from reportlab.lib import colors 290→from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet from reportlab.lib.units import inch from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph, SimpleDocTemplate, Table, TableStyle body = getSampleStyleSheet()["BodyText"] rows = [ [Paragraph("ID", body), Paragraph("Name", body), Paragraph("Notes", body)], [Paragraph("1", body), Paragraph("Widget", body), 300→ Paragraph("Long prose wraps cleanly inside its column instead of spilling over.", body)], ] grid = Table(rows, colWidths=[0.5 * inch, 1.5 * inch, 4.5 * inch], repeatRows=1) grid.setStyle(TableStyle([ ("GRID", (0, 0), (-1, -1), 0.5, colors.grey), ("VALIGN", (0, 0), (-1, -1), "TOP"), ("BACKGROUND", (0, 0), (-1, 0), colors.lightgrey), ])) 310→SimpleDocTemplate("grid.pdf", pagesize=letter).build([grid]) ``` Also: `repeatRows=1` reprints the header when a table crosses a page break; `VALIGN TOP` keeps wrapped rows tidy; and when content is genuinely too wide, switch to `landscape(letter)` rather than shrinking columns into illegibility. ## Always Verify Visually After producing or modifying any PDF — especially after filling form fields, where name-to-label mappings are frequently wrong — render each page and look at it: ```bash 320→pdftoppm -png -r 300 -f 1 -l 1 result.pdf /tmp/check pdftoppm -png -r 300 -f 2 -l 2 result.pdf /tmp/check_p2 ``` pdftoppm appends the page number to the output prefix, so these commands write `/tmp/check-1.png` and `/tmp/check_p2-2.png`. View each PNG and confirm every value sits beside its intended label, nothing overlaps, and nothing is clipped. Inspecting the raw PDF objects cannot catch these problems; rendering does. ## Forms and Tax Forms - Any form-filling task: read `forms.md` first and follow its steps in order. It covers both PDFs with real fillable fields and flat/scanned forms that need positioned text annotations, with helper scripts under `scripts/`. - Tax returns: read `tax.md`. The deliverable is always the official IRS form from `forms/`, filled in — never a homemade summary document. 330→

The code looks good. I will rebuild the PDF and render all pages to verify them.

I am running the build now. I noticed a potential LayoutError risk: if a flowable's split returns an empty list and the next frame cannot fit it either, platypus may loop infinitely.

The 680-point threshold catches only very tall paragraphs. Normal text fits easily.

Calling wrap inside split might corrupt the paragraph's internal state. I am checking reportlab's internal frame logic to confirm.

Reportlab's internal frame logic confirms that calling wrap inside split is safe. The Fix & Fogg URL is 517.7 points wide, so it will break across lines. I am tracing how the URL splits on slashes to find the exact break point.

The Fix & Fogg URL splits into six slash-separated segments. The prefix likely fits on one line, but the query string alone may still overflow the width limit.

The Fix & Fogg URL is only 27 points over the width limit, so it will break cleanly before the final path segment. The Pic URL should split similarly. Nutella fits entirely on one line and will stay unbroken.
